Finite direct sums are coherent by applying the Stacks two-out-of-three assertion to the split short exact sequence and inducting on the finite family.
Parts one and three of the Stacks lemma give coherence of the image kernel and cokernel of a morphism between coherent modules.
The sum is a finite-type submodule and the intersection is the kernel of the quotient map so both conclusions follow from parts one and three of the Stacks lemma.

Coherence of the holomorphic-function sheaf on a complex analytic variety is Oka's analytic theorem and has no algebraic Stacks statement; no tag is assigned.
Stacks proves the structure sheaf coherent for every locally Noetherian scheme which includes algebraic varieties over a field.
When the structure sheaf is coherent Stacks identifies coherent modules exactly with finite-presentation modules equivalently local cokernels of maps between finite free modules.
A submodule of a finite free coherent module is coherent exactly when it is finite type by the definition and part one of the Stacks coherent-category lemma.
The relation sheaf is finite type by coherence and is a submodule of a finite free coherent module so the preceding Stacks result makes it coherent.
Stacks proves the annihilator coherent when the structure sheaf and module are coherent; applying this to the coherent quotient also gives the conductor assertion.

The exact coherent change-of-rings theorem was absent; the new Stacks lemma proves invariance of coherence for modules over a coherent quotient sheaf of rings and proves the quotient coherent over itself.
The new lemma is the source theorem in Stacks form: a module over the quotient by a coherent ideal is coherent over the quotient exactly when it is coherent over the original coherent sheaf of rings.

The existing closed-pushforward lemma already gives the finite-type result in greater generality and is extended under the source's identity-on-rings hypothesis to include coherence and coherence of the ring sheaf itself.
Stacks proves reflection and preservation of finite type for any closed ringed-space morphism with surjective structure map; extension by zero is the special case in which that map is an isomorphism.
The Stacks proof uses the same correspondence of local generators and surjections and also handles a general surjective structure map rather than only extension by zero.

The lemma now records that when the structure sheaf on X is exactly the closed pushforward of the structure sheaf on Z, relation sheaves correspond under exact pushforward, so coherence is preserved and reflected.
Applying the new coherence clause to the structure sheaf gives exactly the source corollary: coherence of the ring sheaf is invariant under closed extension by zero.

The Stacks Cech complex uses the identical alternating restriction-map differential, proves d squared is zero, and defines the same cohomology groups; its alternating cochains form the same subcomplex.
The sheaf axiom is exactly the assertion that degree-zero Cech cohomology for every open covering equals the sections on the covered open, giving the source proposition when that open is X.
The source proves that alternating and unrestricted covering cochains have isomorphic cohomology; Stacks proves the stronger statement that the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence.

The source invokes an abstract dimension-raising simplicial homotopy. Stacks supplies explicit cochain homotopies, including their signs, which establish the same projection-to-alternating comparison and the stronger homotopy-equivalence conclusion.

No named Stacks result stated the source's useful nerve-dimension vanishing bound. The new lemma records it with the necessary sheaf hypothesis, derives it from the alternating-complex homotopy equivalence, and avoids introducing a competing definition of covering dimension.

Stacks defines the same restriction map from a covering to a refinement, proves it commutes with the differential, and records the resulting transition map on covering cohomology, with a later total-complex version for complexes of sheaves.

The existing section proves choice-independence by the same prism homotopy, but its local displayed identity had the sign reversed relative to both the source and its own later detailed calculation. The sign is corrected to gamma-prime minus gamma and a labelled reference note now fixes the ordering convention and the distinction between cochain-level dependence and cohomological independence.

Stacks already constructs the directed refinement system and its transition maps. The integration makes the colimit a labelled definition and records the source's set-sized cofinal presentation by covering families without conflating Cech cohomology with derived-functor cohomology.

The source definition is the modern direct-limit definition of Cech cohomology. Stacks now exposes it as a labelled reusable definition and explicitly preserves the modern check accent that distinguishes this group from sheaf cohomology.

The coveringwise degree-zero result was present but its colimit consequence was not named. The new lemma proves that global sections map isomorphically to degree-zero Cech cohomology by applying the sheaf axiom on every covering and passing through identity transition maps.

Stacks uses functoriality of the Cech complex throughout but had no single labelled result collecting the source's formal consequences. The new lemma proves covariance and additivity, finite-direct-sum compatibility, the natural degree-zero identification, and the canonical module structure over global sections.

The source repairs the failure of right exactness for a fixed-cover Cech complex by inserting its image complex and obtains the low-degree exact sequence after refinement. The new reference remark preserves that construction and identifies its six terms with the stronger modern derived-functor sequence.

The image-complex long exact sequence is source-specific historical machinery. The reference remark records the construction and its refinement compatibility without introducing the auxiliary H_0 groups as a competing modern theory.

The source's degree-zero isomorphism and degree-one injection for its auxiliary image-complex cohomology are preserved in the reference remark and traced to the local lifting criterion for an epimorphism of sheaves.
The source lemma is exactly the local lifting criterion for a surjective morphism of sheaves, organized simultaneously over the members of a covering by taking the union of the local lifting covers.

The source proves the six-term exact sequence for direct-limit Cech cohomology. Degree zero and one agree with derived-functor cohomology, whose universal delta-functor supplies the full long exact sequence in every degree.
The source's surjectivity criterion is the immediate degree-zero consequence of the full derived-functor long exact sequence and is recorded explicitly in the reference remark.

Stacks previously proved the Cech-to-derived comparison only for Hausdorff quasi-compact spaces. The integration adds the source's paracompact refinement mechanism and strengthens the comparison theorem to every paracompact space while retaining the prior compact statement as a corollary.

The source proves that its auxiliary image-complex cohomology maps isomorphically to direct-limit Cech cohomology in every degree on a paracompact space. The strengthened Stacks lemma uses the same simultaneous lifting mechanism to prove the stronger modern conclusion that Cech and derived-functor cohomology agree in every degree.

No Stacks result supplied the source's locally finite simultaneous-refinement argument beyond the quasi-compact case. The new topology lemmas prove a shrinking theorem and the degree-p refinement theorem needed to lift every component of a cochain on one common refinement.

The first neighbourhood condition is retained in the new refinement proof: membership in V_j or W_j permits simultaneous shrinking inside the corresponding open. Direct authority review reverses the inherited false overline in this condition.
The second condition is the star-control step in the new proof: if a chosen neighbourhood meets the shrunken W_j then it lies in V_j, using closure(W_j) contained in V_j and local finiteness.

The third condition combines local finiteness with the local lifting criterion for a sheaf epimorphism; only finitely many index tuples occur near a point, so all required component lifts can be imposed on one neighbourhood.

On a paracompact space the new comparison theorem identifies the source's full exact sequence of direct-limit Cech groups with derived-functor cohomology. The modern derived long exact sequence itself exists for every space, so it is stronger than the source corollary.

The source identifies a sheaf supported on a closed subspace with extension by zero and constructs the restriction map on Cech cochains. Stacks expresses the same construction categorically as the fully faithful exact closed-pushforward functor and its induced cohomology identity.

FAC Proposition 8 states exactly that cohomology is unchanged by extending an abelian sheaf from a closed subspace by zero. The Stacks lemma proves the same identity from exactness of closed pushforward and Leray.

FAC defines a first-quadrant double complex with anticommuting differentials and total differential d-prime plus d-double-prime. Stacks uses commuting squares and inserts the standard sign in the total differential; the two conventions are equivalent by a sign twist, and Stacks develops both associated spectral sequences.

FAC Proposition 1 is the first-quadrant abelian-group case of the second-variable variant of the Stacks resolution lemma: horizontal acyclicity away from degree zero makes the edge complex quasi-isomorphic to the total complex. Stacks proves the result in an arbitrary abelian category under the precise finite-diagonal convergence hypothesis.

Stacks contains the general double-complex and Cech-complex formalisms but no dedicated reusable construction for FAC's double complex attached to two coverings. The new reference remark records the construction with the Stacks commuting-square convention and the corresponding total-complex sign.

The source computes horizontal cohomology as the product of the Cech cohomology groups of the restricted coverings and identifies the degree-zero edge complex with the Cech complex of the other covering. The reference remark preserves this computation and its symmetric counterpart without presenting it as a new tagged theorem.

Stacks had the abstract double-complex resolution lemma, refinement maps, and the derived Leray criterion, but not FAC's Cech-acyclic refinement theorem or its cofinal consequence. The integration adds both reusable statements, proves them with the two-covering complex, and records the source's proposed weakening separately.

FAC Proposition 3 is the horizontal-acyclic edge comparison for its two-covering double complex. The abstract Stacks resolution lemma proves this edge quasi-isomorphism in any abelian category once the source's explicit complex is supplied.

The source proves vanishing of positive Cech cohomology when a covering contains the whole space. The Stacks lemma is stronger: for any abelian presheaf it gives an explicit contraction of the entire augmented Cech complex.

The source proves that the fine-cover edge maps isomorphically to two-covering total cohomology and that the resulting comparison equals the standard refinement homomorphism. The new refinement lemma retains the same explicit edge homotopy, while the existing refinement section supplies functoriality and independence of the refinement function.

FAC Proposition 5 is now a standalone Stacks lemma: a refinement induces an isomorphism on Cech cohomology when its restrictions to every finite intersection of the coarse cover are Cech-acyclic in positive degrees.

FAC Theorem 1 is now a standalone Stacks lemma identifying the Cech cohomology of one covering with the refinement-colimit Cech cohomology when a cofinal family satisfies the restricted-cover acyclicity criterion.

The cofinality hypothesis is retained exactly: every covering admits a refinement in the designated family. The proof explicitly restricts to the still-cofinal subfamily also refining the fixed covering.
The positive-degree Cech-acyclicity of each family member restricted to every finite intersection of the fixed cover is the precise hypothesis passed to the new refinement lemma.

The two closing remarks are preserved together: the unproved proposed weakening is explicitly not promoted, and the comparison with Leray is separated from the modern derived-cohomology acyclic-cover criterion.

The source labels as probable the replacement of pointwise restricted-cover vanishing by vanishing only after passage to the cofinal system. The Stacks remark records the question and the exact point where the present proof still needs pre-colimit edge quasi-isomorphisms.

The source notes the analogy with Leray's acyclic-cover theorem. Stacks proves the modern derived-cohomology comparison by a Cech spectral sequence under vanishing of derived cohomology on all finite intersections; the remark states that this is a different hypothesis from FAC's refinement-colimit criterion.

FAC condition (A) is the modern Noetherian condition. Stacks already contains the definition and all three Noetherian permanence and component conclusions; the integration adds exact source references and the missing finite irreducible-open-cover criterion.
FAC's stationarity of every decreasing sequence of closed subsets is exactly the descending-chain definition of a Noetherian topological space used by Stacks.
The minimum condition on the poset of closed subsets is the standard equivalent well-founded form of the descending-chain condition recorded in the Stacks definition.
The three parts of FAC Proposition 1 are exactly the Stacks quasi-compactness, hereditary Noetherianity, and finite-union lemmas, split into their reusable modern locations.
FAC's quasi-compactness conclusion is part (1) of the Stacks lemma; Stacks additionally records retrocompactness of every subset.
FAC's hereditary condition (A) is exactly the Stacks assertion that every subset of a Noetherian space is Noetherian in its induced topology.
The Stacks finite-union lemma has exactly FAC's conclusion for a finite family of Noetherian subspaces and states it for the induced topology on their union.

The equivalence with pairwise intersection of nonempty opens and the inheritance and density of nonempty open subspaces are now recorded in one reusable topology lemma. Stacks retains its explicit nonempty-space convention, unlike the vacuous empty-space convention implicit in FAC.

Stacks proves that a Noetherian space has finitely many irreducible components and additionally that each contains a nonempty open; its general finite-cover lemma supplies the source's uniqueness assertion after redundant members are removed.

FAC's finite open-cover criterion was used informally elsewhere but had no dedicated topology lemma. It is now stated for a nonempty finite cover and proved directly using the pairwise-open characterization of irreducibility.

Stacks replaces the classical locally closed subset of the closed-point space K^r by affine n-space as a scheme and its locally closed reduced induced subscheme. Exact references and a bridge remark identify the classical regular-function sheaf while preserving the additional nonclosed scheme points and the distinction between reduced and nonreduced closed subschemes.

FAC computes the kernel at a classical point as I(F)O_x for the radical vanishing ideal of a closed algebraic set. The affine closed-immersion construction proves the same stalk quotient for every ring, every ideal, and every scheme point; the bridge remark specializes it to the reduced classical setting.
The source's coordinate-ring localization at the maximal ideal of a K-point is the closed-point case of the Stacks identity O_(Spec(R/I),p/I) = R_p/IR_p for arbitrary primes and arbitrary ideals.

Stacks identifies FAC's classical regular maps with morphisms between the associated reduced locally closed schemes, adds exact historical references and the closed-point/Jacobson factorization argument, and explicitly separates this use of regular from the later technical notion of a regular morphism.
Continuity is the underlying-topological-map part of a morphism of locally ringed spaces and hence of a morphism between the associated schemes.

Pulling every regular germ at the image point back to a regular germ is the classical sheaf-level formulation of the local homomorphism on structure sheaves in the definition of a morphism of locally ringed spaces.

FAC's coordinate criterion is the reduced locally closed finite-type case of the Stacks bijection between morphisms to affine space and tuples of global functions; Jacobson closed-point density plus reduced factorization accounts for the prescribed target V.

Stacks replaces the classical product of locally closed K-point sets by the scheme product over K. Exact references and a bridge remark retain the classical closed-point and regular-function description while distinguishing the finer Zariski topology, additional scheme points, and reduced finite-type scope; perfectness of the algebraically closed ground field guarantees that the product remains reduced.
FAC Proposition 6 is exactly the universal property of the product: a map into U times U-prime is a morphism if and only if its two projections are morphisms.

The forward construction of a product morphism is categorical. FAC's converse is recovered by constant-point sections when both source factors are nonempty; the integration records that necessary hypothesis and the empty-factor failure mode.

Products of two isomorphisms are isomorphisms categorically. The converse in FAC follows for nonempty classical source factors by recovering both component maps and their inverses from constant-point sections, but fails without nonemptiness.

Stacks separates the ingredients of FAC's definition: the associated classical actual-function spaces give reduced finite-type schemes over the algebraically closed ground field, VA_II is separatedness, and the modern Stacks term variety additionally requires integrality.

The classical set, topology, and sheaf definition is retained as provenance while the Stacks formulation uses a scheme with reduced finite-type and separatedness hypotheses; nonclosed scheme points and possible nilpotents remain explicit boundaries.
FAC's topology is the underlying topology of the associated scheme, restricted classically to its closed K-points.

FAC's subsheaf of germs of actual K-valued functions agrees with the structure sheaf on the associated reduced locally closed scheme at closed points, whereas general schemes also retain nonclosed points and nilpotent functions.

Over an algebraically closed field, a finite cover by reduced locally closed affine algebraic sets is the classical presentation of a reduced finite-type scheme; conversely a reduced finite-type scheme admits a finite affine cover of this form on closed points.

FAC's finite gluing proposition is the reduced finite-type closed-point case of the general Stacks gluing construction for locally ringed spaces and schemes, which allows arbitrary index sets satisfying the cocycle data.
The requirement that pairwise overlaps be open is exactly the open-overlap hypothesis in scheme gluing data.
Agreement of the induced structures on overlaps is the identity-form instance of compatible overlap isomorphisms and their cocycle condition.

The unique classical product structure is recovered from the scheme fibre product over K on closed points and regular functions; Stacks supplies the general universal construction and retains the additional nonclosed points.

Because a scheme diagonal is an immersion, FAC's condition that its image be a closed subset is equivalent to the modern requirement that the diagonal be a closed immersion, namely separatedness over K.
The closed-graph condition on every pair of affine charts is the target-local verification of closedness of the diagonal and hence of separatedness.

Stacks places the affine locally closed and projective examples in the more general scheme-theoretic framework of immersions, separated affine and projective space, closed projective subschemes, and finite-type quasi-projective morphisms; FAC's algebraic-fibre-space example remains historical context rather than a lexical identification.
The two remarks record the historical separation analogy and the independence of the closed-diagonal axiom from the finite-chart axiom.

FAC explicitly presents its closed-diagonal axiom as analogous to Hausdorff-type separation in topological, differentiable, and analytic geometry; Stacks records the exact algebraic closed-immersion formulation.

Stacks supplies an explicit affine-space-with-doubled-zero gluing example showing that a scheme assembled from affine charts need not be separated, thereby realizing FAC's assertion that VA_I does not imply VA_II.

Stacks separates FAC's composite discussion into ordinary scheme morphisms, reduced induced locally closed subschemes, immersions, products, permanence of separatedness, and the graph as a semi-diagonal. The integration preserves the reduced-source and nonempty-factor qualifications and the modern terminology collision for regular morphisms.

FAC's regular maps are morphisms between the associated reduced finite-type schemes, characterized by pullback of local regular functions. This classical use of regular remains distinct from the technical Stacks property of a regular morphism.
Continuity is the underlying-topological-map condition in the definition of a morphism of locally ringed spaces and hence of schemes.
Pullback of every regular germ to a regular germ is the classical actual-function formulation of the structure-sheaf map for a morphism between the associated reduced schemes.

Stacks now records FAC's topological constancy lemmas and intersection-of-local-rings formula, while the existing generic-point and dimension statements give the modern scheme-theoretic formulation. The integration keeps irreducibility, integrality, finite type, nonempty-open, and component hypotheses explicit.
The new lemma records that global sections of a constant sheaf on a connected space are exactly its constant values, in the slightly more general set-valued form proved directly in Stacks.

The new definition and lemma prove that every locally constant sheaf of sets on an irreducible space is constant; FAC's abelian-sheaf argument is retained as the historical source case, while the broader statement has its own complete proof.

FAC obtains the function field by proving a sheaf of fraction fields constant on the classical closed-point space. Stacks packages the same invariant at the generic point of an integral scheme and explicitly identifies it with the generic local and residue fields.
Source structure; no independent Stacks object.

FAC proves coherence of the classical local-ring sheaf first on affine space, then for a closed subvariety by its vanishing ideal and quotient, and finally locally for algebraic and prealgebraic varieties. Stacks identifies the classical reduced structure sheaf and proves the corresponding results for every locally Noetherian scheme.
FAC's relation-sheaf calculation on affine space is the polynomial-ring case of the Stacks theorem that the structure sheaf of every locally Noetherian scheme is coherent.

FAC's sheaf J(V) is the ideal sheaf of the reduced closed subscheme defined by I(V). Stacks proves more generally that every quasi-coherent submodule or quotient of a coherent module on a locally Noetherian scheme is coherent.

The classical quotient O/J(V) and local chart argument become the structure sheaf of a reduced locally finite type scheme; Stacks proves its coherence, and that of all locally Noetherian structure sheaves, without a chosen affine embedding.

FAC observes that separatedness is unnecessary by extending Proposition 1 to prealgebraic varieties. The Stacks result is local and applies to arbitrary locally Noetherian schemes, including nonseparated ones.

FAC defines algebraic sheaves and their homomorphisms as modules and module maps over the classical structure sheaf, records the global-section-ring action on cohomology, and characterizes coherence by a local finite presentation. Stacks gives each construction on general ringed spaces and the coherence equivalence on locally Noetherian schemes.
FAC's algebraic sheaf is exactly a sheaf of modules over the classical local-ring sheaf. Stacks makes the same definition for an arbitrary sheaf of rings on any topological space.
FAC's algebraic homomorphism is exactly a morphism of sheaves of O_V-modules. Stacks packages these morphisms and their category for arbitrary ringed spaces.

FAC defines coherence by the general ringed-space relation-sheaf condition and, because O_V is coherent, characterizes it by a local cokernel O_V^q to O_V^p. Stacks proves coherent equals finite-presentation for every locally Noetherian scheme and defines the displayed local presentation explicitly.

FAC treats the ideal of a closed classical subvariety, coherence of that ideal, the exact structure-sheaf quotient, coherent direct image and descent, preservation of cohomology, and power-annihilation for sheaves supported on the subvariety. Stacks gives the corresponding statements for closed immersions and coherent modules on locally Noetherian or Noetherian schemes, while retaining scheme-theoretic structure.

The classical ideal sheaf J(W) is the kernel of O_V to i_*O_W for the reduced closed subscheme associated to W. The modern closed-immersion formulation permits arbitrary quasi-coherent defining ideals and therefore also nonreduced closed subschemes.

FAC proves coherence of J(W) by an affine embedding and finite generation. Stacks proves that every quasi-coherent ideal sheaf, as a submodule of O_X, is coherent on an arbitrary locally Noetherian scheme.

FAC identifies coherent sheaves on W with coherent sheaves on V annihilated by J(W), using closed extension by zero, and records unchanged cohomology. Stacks makes this an equivalence for coherent modules under any closed immersion of locally Noetherian schemes and derives the cohomology identity from exact pushforward.

FAC observes that set-theoretic support on W need only force annihilation by a power of J(W), not by J(W) itself. Stacks proves the converse as well for coherent sheaves on arbitrary Noetherian schemes and quasi-coherent defining ideals.

Stacks already constructs the meromorphic-function sheaf and identifies it with the constant function-field sheaf on an integral scheme. A new lemma records FAC's finite-type criterion for its submodules, the positive-dimensional noncoherence boundary, and the denominator-clearing reduction to a finite type submodule of the coherent structure sheaf.

FAC's sheaf of fractional ideals is an arbitrary O_V-submodule of the constant function-field sheaf. The Stacks bridge uses the meromorphic-function sheaf on an integral scheme and explicitly records that the historical term imposes neither invertibility nor local rank one.

The new lemma proves FAC Proposition 4 for locally Noetherian integral schemes: an O_X-submodule of K_X is coherent exactly when it is of finite type. Its proof clears a common local denominator and invokes coherence of finite type submodules of O_X; it also proves that K_X itself is coherent exactly in dimension zero.

Stacks separates FAC's discussion into the vector-bundle/module anti-equivalence, finite locally free modules and their coherence, differentials of smooth morphisms, algebraic Hodge cohomology and its spectral sequence, and Poincare duality for Weil cohomology. Historical notes record the dual convention and the extra comparison needed for topological Betti numbers.

The sheaf of regular sections of a classical rank-r bundle is finite locally free of rank r. Under the Stacks convention V(E)=Spec(Sym(E)), the degree-one module is dual to the classical section sheaf, so the corresponding geometric bundle is V(S(E)^vee).

FAC Proposition 5 and its converse identify classical rank-r vector bundles with locally free sheaves of rank r and deduce coherence. Stacks gives the vector-bundle anti-equivalence for arbitrary quasi-coherent modules; after restricting to finite locally free modules and applying the dual convention, it recovers the classical equivalence and the coherence conclusion.

FAC's h^(p,q) is the dimension of H^q(V,Omega^p) for a nonsingular projective variety. Stacks defines the same groups as the bidegree pieces of algebraic Hodge cohomology and places them on the first page of the Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence; finiteness and numerical dimensions require the proper finite-type hypotheses used later.

The formula B_n=sum_(p+q=n) h^(p,q) is recalled from complex Hodge theory and proposed speculatively as a definition in the general case. Stacks defines the algebraic Hodge direct sum but does not identify its dimension with a topological or etale Betti number without additional comparison, degeneration, and characteristic hypotheses.

FAC records the numerical symmetry B_n=B_(2m-n) for an irreducible nonsingular projective variety of dimension m. The Stacks Weil-cohomology lemma proves the underlying perfect duality for every nonempty smooth projective equidimensional scheme under the stated Weil-cohomology axioms, and hence the corresponding dimension symmetry.
Source structure; no independent Stacks object.

Stacks supplies scheme-theoretic versions of every construction in FAC no. 42: affine objects, products and closed subobjects, affine opens and principal opens, standard-open bases, affine refinements, and the separatedness criterion governing affine intersections. The modern statements work over arbitrary rings or schemes with their stated hypotheses and retain nonclosed points and scheme structure.

FAC defines an affine classical variety as a closed subvariety of affine space and records closure under products and closed subvarieties. Stacks defines affine schemes intrinsically as spectra, identifies affine varieties with the integral finite-type case, and proves the product and closed-immersion statements without discarding scheme structure; FAC's broader reducible variety convention remains explicit.

FAC equips an open subset with its induced classical-variety structure and calls it affine when that object is affine. Stacks gives every open subspace its canonical open-subscheme structure and uses the same affine-scheme condition, for arbitrary schemes.

FAC proves affine intersections by the closed diagonal and notes failure without its separatedness axiom. Stacks proves the relative statement for every separated morphism and explicitly records that two affine opens of a general scheme need not have affine intersection.

FAC's V_f is the locus of classical points where a regular function is nonzero. On the associated reduced scheme it is exactly D(f), the open locus where the germ is a unit; for an affine scheme this agrees with the standard open.

FAC proves V_f affine by the graph equation lambda f=1 in V times affine one-space. Stacks identifies D(f) with Spec(R_f), proving the assertion over an arbitrary ring and retaining the full scheme structure.

FAC uses polynomials vanishing on a closed set to obtain a basis of principal opens in its complement. The spectrum theorem gives the intrinsic standard-open basis for every ring and includes all prime points, with the classical statement recovered on the reduced finite-type closed-point space.

FAC proves that affine opens form a basis by locally embedding a classical variety in affine space. In Stacks this is built into local affineness and holds for every scheme, with standard affine neighbourhoods available inside each open subspace.

FAC's phrase arbitrarily fine means that every open covering admits an affine refinement. Stacks gives that basis statement for all schemes and a finite standard refinement over an affine member; FAC's additional finite-intersection assertion is recovered under separatedness, not for arbitrary schemes.

FAC no. 43 proves affine global sections and two power-denominator statements by local affine reduction, Nullstellensatz, finite presentation, and local lifting. Stacks proves the global-section identity for every affine scheme and packages both power statements in localization of global sections of any quasi-coherent module on a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme.

FAC proves that the coordinate ring of an irreducible closed classical subvariety over an algebraically closed field is its ring of regular functions, while noting irreducibility is unnecessary. Stacks identifies global sections of Spec(A), and of every associated module, directly for an arbitrary ring; the history records the circular ordering of one printed equality in the FAC proof.

FAC clears a uniform power of Q from a regular function on X_Q using a finite affine cover and Nullstellensatz. Stacks proves Gamma(X,O_X)_Q isomorphic to Gamma(X_Q,O_X) for every quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme, which gives exactly the extension after multiplying by a power and removes irreducibility and finite-type hypotheses.

FAC proves that a global section of a coherent algebraic sheaf vanishing on X_Q is killed by a high power of Q. The kernel statement for localization in the Stacks lemma proves this for every quasi-coherent module on a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme, so coherence and irreducibility are unnecessary.

FAC reduces locally to a closed classical subvariety of affine space and then uses a finite affine cover to globalize an exponent. Stacks instead uses the affine-open basis and the intrinsic Spec construction, with quasi-compactness supplying the finite uniformization step.

FAC locally presents a coherent sheaf as the cokernel of a map between finite free sheaves. Stacks proves every coherent module is of finite presentation and, on the locally Noetherian schemes corresponding to classical varieties, identifies coherence with the required finite-presentation behavior.

FAC shrinks locally so that a section of the cokernel lifts to a section of the finite free source. Stacks proves the relevant local-surjectivity and local-lifting mechanism for finite type target modules on arbitrary ringed spaces.

FAC clears pointwise denominators, uses Nullstellensatz to place a high power of Q in their ideal, and uses quasi-compactness for a uniform exponent. Stacks packages the same denominator and torsion calculations in the kernel and surjectivity of localization of global sections on a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme.

FAC no. 44 proves vanishing of higher Cech cohomology for a finite principal-open cover, passes to higher sheaf cohomology, deduces exactness of global sections, and recovers the coordinate ring of an arbitrary closed classical subvariety. Stacks proves each step for arbitrary quasi-coherent modules on affine schemes and records the cofinal-cover passage explicitly.

FAC constructs an explicit contracting cochain after clearing powers of the covering functions for a coherent subsheaf of O_X^p on an irreducible affine classical variety. Stacks proves higher Cech cohomology zero for every quasi-coherent module and every finite standard-open cover of any affine scheme; its alternating homotopy also exposes the printed q-versus-j sign defect.

FAC uses the cofinality of its principal-open covers to pass from Proposition 7 to H^q(X,F)=0. Stacks makes this Cech-to-derived-cohomology passage explicit and proves affine vanishing for every quasi-coherent module without irreducibility or coherence assumptions.

FAC derives surjectivity of Gamma(O_X^p) to Gamma(O_X^p/F) from H^1(X,F)=0. On an affine scheme Stacks identifies quasi-coherent sheaves with modules, preserves kernels and cokernels, and hence gives exactness of global sections for all quasi-coherent short exact sequences.

FAC applies Corollary 2 on affine space to prove that every regular function on an arbitrary closed classical subvariety comes from its coordinate ring. Stacks identifies Gamma(Spec(A),O) with A directly for every ring, including reducible and nonreduced affine schemes.

FAC no. 45 proves stalkwise generation by global sections, extension from a principal open after multiplying by a power, finite global generation for coherent sheaves, and exactness of global sections. Stacks obtains all four conclusions from the affine quasi-coherent module correspondence and localization, under weaker hypotheses and without the classical irreducibility reduction.

FAC proves that global sections generate every stalk of a coherent algebraic sheaf on an affine classical variety. Stacks identifies every quasi-coherent module on an arbitrary affine scheme with the sheaf associated to its global-section module, whose localizations are generated by the images of those global sections; coherence, irreducibility, reducedness, and finite type are unnecessary.

FAC patches across a finite principal-open cover to show that a section over X_Q becomes the restriction of a global section after multiplication by Q to a high power. Stacks proves directly that Gamma(X,F)_Q maps isomorphically to Gamma(X_Q,F) for every quasi-coherent module on a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme.

FAC uses finite stalk generators and quasi-compactness to obtain a surjection O_X^p to a coherent sheaf on an affine classical variety. Stacks identifies a finite type quasi-coherent sheaf on an affine scheme with a finite module; any finite generating set of that module sheafifies to the required finite free surjection, without irreducibility or reducedness assumptions.

FAC proves exactness of global sections for a sequence of coherent algebraic sheaves on an affine variety by resolving the image with a finite free sheaf. Stacks makes global sections part of an exact equivalence between quasi-coherent modules on an affine scheme and modules over its coordinate ring, and preserves the relevant kernels and images; coherence is unnecessary.

FAC no. 46 extends principal-cover Cech vanishing from an irreducible finite-free-subsheaf case to arbitrary coherent sheaves on affine classical varieties, then derives affine sheaf-cohomology vanishing and a global-section lifting result. Stacks proves the Cech and sheaf-cohomology statements for every quasi-coherent module on any affine scheme and isolates the lifting obstruction for arbitrary short exact sequences.

FAC proves positive-degree Cech vanishing for a coherent algebraic sheaf and a finite principal-open cover of an arbitrary affine classical variety, first resolving the irreducible case by a finite free sheaf and then using a closed embedding for the general case. Stacks proves the same result directly for every quasi-coherent module and every finite standard-open cover of an arbitrary affine scheme.

FAC passes from its cofinal family of finite principal-open coverings to vanishing of higher sheaf cohomology for coherent algebraic sheaves on affine varieties. Stacks verifies the basis and cofinality conditions explicitly and proves affine vanishing for all quasi-coherent modules without classical irreducibility, reducedness, or finite-type hypotheses.

FAC uses H^1(X,A)=0 to show that global sections of B surject onto those of C in a short exact sequence whose kernel A is coherent on an affine variety; it imposes no coherence hypothesis on B or C. FAC no. 47 proves Cech vanishing and Cech-to-sheaf-cohomology comparison for finite affine-open covers, then uses kernel-coherent lifting to identify its auxiliary image complex and obtain a long exact sequence. Stacks already has the stronger affine-intersection comparison and derived-functor long exact sequence; the integration extends the historical image-complex record without creating a competing cohomology theory.

FAC refines a finite affine-open cover of an affine classical variety by principal opens and proves positive-degree Cech vanishing. Stacks uses affineness of all finite intersections to identify Cech cohomology with sheaf cohomology, then applies affine vanishing; the result holds for any quasi-coherent module and does not require a finite cover.

FAC proves that a finite affine-open cover of a classical algebraic variety computes cohomology of a coherent algebraic sheaf by its cofinal-refinement criterion. Stacks obtains the same comparison from the Cech spectral sequence whenever every finite intersection is affine, including any affine cover of a separated scheme, and needs only quasi-coherence.

FAC proves that its source-specific image subcomplex C_0 equals the ordinary Cech complex for the quotient sheaf on a finite affine-open cover because the coherent kernel has vanishing H^1 on every affine intersection. FAC passes the fixed-cover image-complex comparison to the refinement colimit and identifies H_0^q(X,C) with its Cech cohomology. This auxiliary construction is preserved in the historical remark and cofinal-refinement record but is not introduced as a separate modern invariant.

FAC obtains the long exact sequence by combining its image-complex exact sequence with the preceding all-degree comparison under a coherent-kernel hypothesis. FAC identifies a classical affine variety over the fixed algebraically closed field with the character space of its reduced finitely generated coordinate algebra. FAC proves exactness of its associated-sheaf functor by identifying each classical stalk with a localization of the coordinate ring. Stacks proves exactness of M maps to tilde M for every ring and every prime stalk, with localization exactness providing the algebraic mechanism.

FAC constructs module fractions, identifies A_S tensor_A M with M_S, and proves exactness for a multiplicative set excluding zero. Stacks gives the same fraction proof for arbitrary multiplicative subsets, including the zero-ring localization when zero belongs to the set.

FAC detects M from vanishing of its associated sheaf by testing classical closed-point stalks and using the maximal ideals of its finite-type coordinate ring. Stacks has the stronger identity Gamma(Spec(A),tilde M)=M and an equivalence with quasi-coherent modules for every ring.

FAC uses Noetherianity of the finite-type coordinate algebra to present a finite module by finite free modules and concludes that its associated sheaf is coherent. Stacks characterizes coherent modules on every locally Noetherian scheme and isolates the necessary finite-presentation condition.

FAC no. 49 constructs the global-section module, proves that associated sheaf and global sections are quasi-inverse on finite modules and coherent sheaves over a classical affine variety, and warns that projective space requires a modified correspondence. FAC makes global sections a covariant module functor, proves its exactness on coherent sheaves over a classical affine variety by no. 45, and shows the module is finite. FAC states that associated sheaf and global sections are inverse on the finite-module and coherent-sheaf subcategories of a classical affine variety. Stacks gives natural quasi-inverse equivalences between every module over an arbitrary ring and every quasi-coherent module on its affine spectrum.

FAC proves Gamma(A(M)) is canonically M for finite modules. Stacks proves Gamma(Spec(R),tilde M)=M functorially for every module over every ring, without finite generation, reducedness, or finite-type hypotheses.

FAC proves that the sheaf associated to the global sections of a coherent algebraic sheaf is canonically the original sheaf. Stacks proves the counit isomorphism for every quasi-coherent module on an arbitrary affine scheme, without coherence or Noetherianity.

FAC proves the unit isomorphism first for finite free modules and then for finite modules using a two-row finite-free presentation diagram plus exactness of both associated sheaf and affine global sections. FAC no. 50 links projective modules, stalkwise freeness, locally free coherent sheaves, and classical vector bundles over an affine variety, then records the 1955 polynomial-ring question. FAC tests a finite module over a classical affine coordinate ring by freeness at every classical closed-point stalk. Stacks proves the equivalent finite-projective criterion over any ring using localizations at every prime or every maximal ideal and makes finite presentation explicit.

FAC proves the converse through the historical equality between global projective dimension and the supremum of the projective dimensions of its classical localizations. FAC gives three equivalent conditions for a coherent sheaf on a connected classical affine variety. Stacks separates finite local freeness on arbitrary schemes from the vector-bundle anti-equivalence and removes connectedness except when one wants a single constant rank.

FAC asks that the global-section module be projective in its finite coherent affine setting. Stacks identifies global sections under the full affine quasi-coherent equivalence and characterizes finite projective modules over any ring.

FAC requires local isomorphisms to O^p with p constant on the connected variety. Stacks defines locally free modules on arbitrary ringed spaces and gives equivalent finite locally free criteria with rank only locally constant in general.

FAC identifies the sheaf with the regular-section sheaf of a finite-rank classical fibre space. Stacks gives an anti-equivalence between quasi-coherent modules and relative-spectrum vector bundles, with the dual convention explicitly recorded.

FAC states a bijection on isomorphism classes between finite projective modules and classical vector bundles, with free corresponding to trivial. Stacks upgrades the affine module-sheaf step and the sheaf-bundle step to categorical equivalences, subject to the relative-spectrum dual convention.

FAC records as open in 1955 whether finite projective modules over a polynomial ring over a field are free. Quillen--Suslin later answered this affirmatively, but the theorem is not developed in the current Stacks snapshot; no official tag is assigned.

FAC starts with the scalar action of K-star on the punctured affine space and forms an orbit set. Stacks constructs projective space by Proj and represents its full functor of points; the scalar action remains the classical closed-point lineage rather than the definition of the scheme.

FAC defines P_r(K) as equivalence classes of nonzero coordinate vectors. Stacks defines projective n-space over Z by Proj, base changes it over any scheme, and gives its functorial line-bundle description, retaining nonclosed and scheme-valued points.

FAC's coordinate functions t_i on affine space become the degree-one polynomial generators T_i in the Proj construction. They are homogeneous coordinates, not global regular scalar-valued functions on projective space.

FAC covers the classical quotient by loci where one coordinate is nonzero. Stacks identifies these with the standard opens D_+(T_i), proves the standard-open topology for every graded ring, and obtains the cover over Z and every base change.

FAC uses the ratios t_j/t_i to give a bijection from each U_i to K^r and then proves it biregular. Stacks identifies the whole standard open as Spec of the degree-zero localization, canonically affine n-space over the base.

FAC defines regular functions by scalar-invariant functions upstairs and locally by same-degree homogeneous fractions P/Q. Stacks constructs the structure sheaf on all homogeneous prime points from the rings S_(f), proves its restriction and stalk formulas, and identifies every standard open with an affine scheme.

FAC verifies its two classical variety axioms using affine charts and closed transition graphs. Stacks proves Proj is a scheme for every graded ring, proves separatedness separately, and specializes the standard affine cover to projective space over arbitrary bases.

FAC calls a classical variety projective when it is isomorphic to a closed subvariety of some projective space. Stacks defines projectivity intrinsically through the structure morphism and proves the equivalent closed-subscheme characterization, while its variety convention imposes integrality and its scheme language retains structure beyond closed points.

FAC no. 52 computes coherent cohomology from the standard projective cover, bounds it first by ambient dimension and then by support dimension, and proves the latter through homogeneous principal opens and a Veronese argument. Stacks separates these ingredients into affine-intersection Cech comparison, finite-cover vanishing, Grothendieck vanishing on Noetherian spaces, and the direct Proj localization and Veronese-subring constructions.

FAC proves that the finite standard affine cover of classical projective space computes coherent sheaf cohomology. Stacks proves the comparison for any quasi-coherent module and any open cover whose finite intersections are affine, with no restriction to projective space or a finite index set.

FAC obtains H^n(P_r(K),F)=0 for n>r from its r+1 standard charts. Stacks gives the finite-affine-cover bound for every quasi-coherent module on a quasi-compact scheme with affine diagonal and records the projective-space specialization over every Noetherian base ring.

FAC proves vanishing above the dimension of the support for coherent sheaves on classical quasi-projective varieties. Grothendieck vanishing in Stacks applies to every abelian sheaf on a Noetherian topological space; applying it to the closed support and using exact closed pushforward removes the coherence and quasi-projective restrictions.

FAC specializes Proposition 3 to W=V and obtains vanishing above dim V. Stacks proves this for every abelian sheaf on every Noetherian topological space, so the classical finite-type variety and coherent-module hypotheses are unnecessary for the vanishing bound.

FAC constructs k+1 positive-degree homogeneous polynomials vanishing on the projective boundary and without a common zero on the k-dimensional support. This dimension-lowering construction is recorded as the source's special proof route to support-dimension vanishing; the modern target proves the stronger theorem without requiring projective equations.

FAC proves that the nonvanishing locus of a positive-degree homogeneous polynomial on classical projective space is affine by a Veronese embedding. Stacks identifies D_+(f) directly with Spec(S_(f)) for every graded ring, retaining nonclosed points and arbitrary bases.

FAC uses the map given by all degree-n monomials and its closed classical Veronese image to reduce the nonvanishing locus to a hyperplane complement. Stacks records the canonical Proj isomorphism for the Veronese subring and proves standard-open affineness directly; these are related ingredients but the subring isomorphism alone is not silently promoted to the ambient closed-immersion assertion.

FAC covers the chosen open neighbourhood by homogeneous principal affine opens, with only k+1 members capable of meeting the support simultaneously, and computes cohomology by the resulting Cech complex. Stacks retains each ingredient separately and obtains the final bound more generally from Grothendieck vanishing.

FAC uses alternating cochains indexed by distinct cover members, so the degree-n group is zero once n exceeds the k+1 support-relevant members. Stacks proves the alternating complex is homotopy equivalent to the usual Cech complex and uses the identical degree-counting argument in its finite-affine-cover vanishing lemma.

FAC no. 53 proves higher direct-limit Cech vanishing on a classical irreducible curve from a cofinal system of finite-complement covers and the acyclicity of a finite simplex. Stacks now records that proof lineage beside its distinct derived-functor vanishing theorem and its general alternating-complex and simplicial-contraction results.

FAC introduces covers B_F whose members restore one point at a time to the complement of a finite closed-point set. The construction is retained as the source's curve-specific cofinal system for its direct-limit Cech theory, not promoted to a general Stacks theorem.

FAC proves that the finite-complement covers are cofinal by collecting the finite complements of a given cover and assigning each point of their union to a covering member. Stacks supplies general refinement and cofinality formalism, but its stated hypotheses are not asserted to be an exact reformulation of this curve lemma.

FAC identifies the positive-degree alternating Cech complex of B_F with the cochain complex of the simplex on F and concludes that its cohomology vanishes in degrees at least two. Stacks contains the general alternating-to-usual comparison and the standard simplex contraction; the source's coefficient-system identification remains historical proof data.

The displayed vanishing follows from acyclicity of the nonempty finite simplex after identifying every positive multiple intersection with the whole curve and hence every coefficient group with Gamma(V,F). The Stacks labels record the two reusable ingredients without suppressing the degree truncation or the sheaf-theoretic identification.

FAC proves vanishing in degrees at least two for its direct-limit Cech groups of an abelian sheaf on a classical irreducible algebraic curve. Stacks proves the stronger derived-functor vanishing theorem for every abelian sheaf on any Noetherian topological space of dimension at most one, while the notation remark prevents an unproved identification of the two theories.

FAC records that the author did not know an arbitrary-dimensional analogue of the preceding curve result. Grothendieck vanishing later gives the derived-functor analogue on all finite-dimensional Noetherian spaces, but this history is not stated as an exact answer for the source's direct-limit Cech groups without a comparison theorem.

FAC glues the restrictions of F on the standard charts with the cocycle (t_j/t_i)^n. For the standard graded polynomial ring, Stacks defines O(n) as the sheaf associated to S(n), defines F(n)=F tensor O(n), and proves that these twists are invertible and their multiplication maps are isomorphisms.

On D_+(t_i), t_i^n is the local generator of O(n), and changing from the jth generator to the ith multiplies coefficients by (t_j/t_i)^n. This is exactly FAC's theta_ij(n), with the source and target order retained so the sign convention is not reversed.

FAC's canonical isomorphisms F(0)=F and F(n)(m)=F(n+m), together with exactness of twisting, are the degree-one-generated Proj case of the Stacks multiplication isomorphisms and the tensor autoequivalence attached to an invertible module.
